proxy_language: Classical Latin (with Etruscan as secondary substrate for Etruria)
proxy_rationale: The Seven-Hills Court (Rome, Latium, Etruria; later court period) is best matched by attested Classical/Republican-Imperial Latin, a richly documented language with full grammars, dictionaries and inscriptions. Etruscan (also attested, but only partly understood) is a defensible secondary proxy for Etruria-flavoured names. Latin is the primary proxy because the 'Seven Hills' court is Roman.
phonology: Classical Latin vowels: short a e i o u and long ā ē ī ō ū; diphthongs ae, au, oe (rare: eu, ui). Consonants: stops p b t d c/k g (c always /k/), qu /kw/, gu /gw/ (after n); fricatives f s h (weak); nasals m n; liquids l r; glides i /j/ and v /w/; x /ks/; z only in Greek loans; ph th ch rare in Greek loans. Stress is penultimate if the penult is heavy (long vowel or closed syllable), else antepenultimate; stress is not written. Etruscan (secondary): 4 vowels a e i u, voiceless stops with aspirates (θ φ χ), s ś z, m n l r, v.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes (C)(C)V(C)(C); onset clusters of stop or f + l/r (pl, bl, cl, gl, fl, pr, br, tr, dr, cr, gr, fr), s + stop (sp, st, sc), sc/sp/st + r/l (str, spl, scr); no word-initial ng, nn, ll, rr. Word-final consonants limited to -s, -m, -t, -r, -l, -n, -c, -d; native words rarely end in -p, -b, -g, -f. Nominatives end in -a, -us, -um, -er, -is, -s/-x, -or, -o/-io, -es. Intervocalic h essentially absent; gemination (ll, ss, tt, nn, rr, cc) occurs word-internally.
orthography: Standard classical Latin spelling in lowercase Latin script: letters a b c d e f g h i k(rare) l m n o p q r s t u v x y z. Use v for consonantal u (vir, Venus, via); i serves for both vowel and glide (Iuppiter, Iulius), though j may be used by older convention. Macrons for long vowels are optional and not part of normal spelling. No w. Digraphs/clusters: qu, gu, ph, th, ch (Greek), ae, oe, au.
morphology: Highly inflected, suffixing. Five declensions (1st -a/-ae; 2nd -us/-um, -er/-ī; 3rd consonant and i-stems with -is genitive; 4th -us/-ūs; 5th -ēs/-eī). Cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative, vocative (locative relic). Three genders. Adjectives agree in gender, number and case. Verbs: four conjugations, tense/mood/voice suffixes. Derivation by suffix: -tor/-trix (agent: aedificator 'builder', victrix), -ium (collective/place/abstract: collegium), -ia (abstract: Victoria), -ilis/-bilis (adjective: nobilis), -ensis (of a place: Romanus, Hostiensis), -arius (professional: faber, aquarius 'water-man'), -ulus/-olus/-culus (diminutive: parvulus), -etum (grove: arbustum, quercetum), -ina (workshop/place: tabernina, officina), -men/-mentum (result/instrument: flumen, fundamentum), -tas (abstract: libertas). Prefixes: in-, con-, per-, pro-, sub-, ab-, ex-.
compounding: True compounding is rare and mostly poetic or Greek-influenced (agricola 'field-tiller', signifer 'standard-bearer', armiger, aedifex, triumvir). Noun compounds typically have a linking -i- (agri-cola, sacri-fex, pontifex 'bridge-maker'), head last. Normal naming uses a head noun plus genitive ('Templum Solis' temple of the Sun, 'Porta Capena', 'Via Appia' by adjective) or noun plus adjective ('Mare Nostrum', 'Forum Romanum', 'Mons Palatinus'). 'Y-maker' is expressed by -tor/-ifex/-fex/-arius derivatives or genitive plus agent noun; Etruscan secondary: genitive in -s/-si/-l, suffix -ale/-ial.
noun_phrase_order: Flexible, but unmarked is head noun first for place/institution names with a genitive or adjective following (Templum Iovis, Aqua Marcia, Forum Boarium, Domus Aurea). Adjectives of quality often precede the noun in literary prose; numerals and demonstratives precede. Genitive dependent normally follows the head. Agreement of gender/number/case is mandatory, so name builders must inflect adjectives to match (nominative singular: aqua clara, mons altus, templum magnum, porta nova).

notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic; here Latin forms are shared by no Goidelic words except established loans, so check against Gaelic lists. Use Latin primarily; for Etruscan-flavoured names use attested Etruscan roots (e.g. lauchume 'king', zilath 'magistrate', tular 'boundary', spur 'city', avil 'year') and its Etruscan-style endings, mark as secondary. The current game strings (Gelsora hirlada, Dehire foga, Pibo, Tadil, Figabe, Tapsu) are not Latin-shaped; they should be replaced with real inflected Latin words or phrases. Keep final consonants within the allowed set and ensure adjective-noun gender agreement.
